prompt: How are the coefficients a_1 to a_6 of the AH_2 molecular orbitals found?

choices.text: By solving the secular determinant
By counting the valence electrons on A
choices.why: The electron count decides which orbitals are filled, not what they are made of. The coefficients come from solving the secular determinant.

choices.text: By measuring them in a photoelectron spectrum
choices.why: PES measures ionization energies, which reflect orbital energies, not coefficients. The coefficients come from solving the secular determinant.

choices.text: By setting all six equal, by symmetry
choices.why: Symmetry ties only the two H coefficients together; A's coefficients differ from them. All of them are found by solving the secular determinant.

explanation: As in earlier molecular orbital problems, the coefficients of the LCAO expansion are found by solving the secular determinant. Symmetry simplifies the job: the two H coefficients must be equal in size, and in linear AH_2 the 2p_x and 2p_y orbitals drop out of the σ orbitals.

prompt: In quantum chemistry, what are the delocalized molecular orbitals that spread over a whole molecule called?

choices.text: Canonical orbitals
Hybrid orbitals
choices.why: Hybrids are mixtures of orbitals on one atom, used to build two-centered bonds. Orbitals delocalized over the whole molecule are called canonical orbitals.

choices.text: Atomic orbitals
choices.why: Atomic orbitals belong to single atoms. The molecular orbitals made by combining them across the whole molecule are the canonical orbitals.

choices.text: Localized bond orbitals
choices.why: Localized orbitals sit on one bond or atom, the opposite of delocalized. Orbitals spread over the whole molecule are called canonical orbitals.

explanation: The molecular orbitals found by the LCAO method spread over the whole molecule, and in a quantum chemical interpretation they are called canonical orbitals. Walsh diagrams follow the energies of these orbitals.

prompt: For an AH_2 molecule whose central atom A uses n = 2 valence orbitals (as Be or O does), which atomic orbitals go into the LCAO?

choices.text: A's 2s and three 2p orbitals, and each H's 1s
A's 2s orbital and each H's 1s, but no 2p
choices.why: A's 2p orbitals belong in the combination as well. The full set is the two H 1s orbitals plus A's 2s, 2p_x, 2p_y and 2p_z.

choices.text: A's three 2p orbitals and each H's 1s, but no 2s
choices.why: A's 2s orbital is included too; it forms the lowest bonding orbital, 2σ_g. The full set is the two H 1s orbitals plus A's 2s and three 2p orbitals.

choices.text: A's 2s and 2p orbitals, and each H's 1s and 2s
choices.why: Each hydrogen donates just its 1s orbital. With A's four n = 2 orbitals, that makes six atomic orbitals in all.

explanation: Each H donates a 1s orbital and A donates its four n = 2 orbitals (2s, 2p_x, 2p_y and 2p_z). Each molecular orbital |χ⟩ is a combination of these six atomic orbitals, with coefficients found by solving the secular determinant.

prompt: In a linear AH_2 molecule with its bonds along the z-axis, why are A's 2p_x and 2p_y orbitals nonbonding?

choices.text: They point perpendicular to the bonds
They are always empty in AH_2 molecules
choices.why: Being filled or empty doesn't make an orbital bonding or not. 2p_x and 2p_y point at right angles to the A–H bonds, so they have no net overlap with the H 1s orbitals.

choices.text: They are much lower in energy than H 1s
choices.why: Energy isn't the reason here. They point at right angles to the bonds, so their overlap with the H 1s orbitals cancels.

choices.text: They are used up in forming sp hybrids
choices.why: This section uses molecular orbitals, not hybrids. 2p_x and 2p_y stay unchanged, as the nonbonding 1π_u pair, because they point perpendicular to the bonds.

explanation: Only A's 2p_z points along the bond axis and overlaps the H 1s orbitals. The 2p_x and 2p_y orbitals point at right angles to the bonds, so they stay unchanged as the nonbonding 1π_u orbitals; this holds only for linear AH_2.

prompt: The section works out the orbitals of AH_2 for a linear geometry, yet water is bent. Why is the linear case still a useful guide to water?

choices.text: Bending reorders the levels only somewhat
Water is really linear in its ground state
choices.why: Water is bent, with an angle of about 104°. The linear case is useful because bending changes the orbital ordering only somewhat.

choices.text: Bending has no effect on the orbital energies
choices.why: It does change them; that is exactly what a Walsh diagram plots. The changes are modest enough that the linear picture stays qualitatively right.

choices.text: The linear orbitals are exact for every AH_2 molecule
choices.why: They are approximate LCAO orbitals, and their energies change with the bond angle. The linear case is kept because its qualitative picture carries over to bent molecules.

explanation: Going from the linear to the bent geometry changes the ordering of the orbitals somewhat, but the qualitative picture from the linear case carries over, which makes it a useful construction for a bent molecule such as H2O.

prompt: According to the section, which two things set how large A's 2s contribution is compared with the hydrogen 1s contributions?

choices.text: A's nuclear charge and the A–H electronegativity gap
The bond angle and the number of lone pairs on A
choices.why: These affect shape, not the mixing amplitudes. The section names A's nuclear charge and the electronegativity difference between H and A.

choices.text: A's atomic mass and the distance between the H atoms
choices.why: Mass plays no part in orbital mixing. It is A's nuclear charge, which sets how fast its 2s orbital decays, and the electronegativity difference.

choices.text: The number of unpaired electrons on A and on H
choices.why: Unpaired electrons are a valence bond idea. The mixing amplitudes depend on A's nuclear charge and the A–H electronegativity difference.

explanation: The nuclear charge of A sets how quickly its 2s orbital decays, and the electronegativity difference between H and A sets how large A's coefficients are compared with the H 1s coefficients.

prompt: In linear AH_2, which description fits the 2σ_g orbital?

choices.text: A's 2s in phase with both H 1s: bonding
A's 2p_z with the out-of-phase H 1s pair: bonding
choices.why: That is 1σ_u, which is ungerade. 2σ_g is the even orbital made from A's 2s and both H 1s orbitals in phase.

choices.text: A's 2s out of phase with both H 1s: antibonding
choices.why: That is 3σ_g, the antibonding partner of 2σ_g. 2σ_g has A's 2s in phase with the two H 1s orbitals.

choices.text: A's 2p_x alone: nonbonding
choices.why: That is one of the 1π_u orbitals. 2σ_g is the bonding orbital made from A's 2s and both H 1s orbitals.

explanation: 2σ_g combines A's 2s with the two H 1s orbitals, all in phase, so it is purely bonding. It is even (gerade) and is built from a 2s orbital, hence the label 2σ_g.

prompt: Why does A's 2p_z orbital combine with the out-of-phase pair of H 1s orbitals rather than the in-phase pair?

choices.text: Its two lobes have opposite signs, like that pair
2p_z is gerade, like the in-phase pair
choices.why: 2p_z changes sign through the center, so it is ungerade. It matches the out-of-phase pair, giving the σ_u orbitals.

choices.text: The in-phase pair is taken by 2p_x and 2p_y
choices.why: 2p_x and 2p_y point away from the bonds and stay nonbonding. The in-phase pair goes with A's 2s; 2p_z matches the out-of-phase pair by symmetry.

choices.text: Out-of-phase pairs always give the lowest energies
choices.why: Sign patterns, not a rule about energy, decide this. The 2p_z lobes on either side of A have opposite signs, just like the out-of-phase H pair.

explanation: Orbitals combine only if they have the same symmetry. 2p_z is positive on one side of A and negative on the other (ungerade), so it pairs with the out-of-phase H combination, giving the bonding 1σ_u and the antibonding 2σ_u orbitals.

prompt: Linear AH_2 has six molecular orbitals: 2σ_g, 1σ_u, two 1π_u, 2σ_u and 3σ_g. How many of them are antibonding?
explanation: 2σ_g and 1σ_u are bonding and the two 1π_u orbitals are nonbonding, which leaves 2 antibonding orbitals: 3σ_g (partner of 2σ_g) and 2σ_u (partner of 1σ_u).

prompt: In Table 10.3.1, water's 2a_1 orbital has an O 2s coefficient of 0.884 and a coefficient of 0.315 on each H 1s orbital. How many times larger is the O 2s coefficient than each H coefficient? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: 0.884 ÷ 0.315 = 2.81. Oxygen's orbital dominates 2a_1, one sign that oxygen takes more than its fair share of the electron density in water's low-lying bonding orbitals.

prompt: BeH2 has four valence electrons. Which of its molecular orbitals do they fill?

choices.text: 2σ_g and 1σ_u (both bonding)
2σ_g and 1π_u (bonding and nonbonding)
choices.why: 1π_u, the nonbonding pair from Be's 2p_x and 2p_y, lies above 1σ_u. Four electrons fill the two bonding orbitals, 2σ_g and 1σ_u.

choices.text: 1π_u only (the nonbonding pair)
choices.why: Nonbonding electrons would give no bond at all. The section's bond order of 2 comes from filling the bonding 2σ_g and 1σ_u orbitals.

choices.text: 2σ_g and 3σ_g (bonding and antibonding)
choices.why: 3σ_g is antibonding, so filling it would cancel the bonding from 2σ_g. The four electrons go into the two bonding orbitals, 2σ_g and 1σ_u.

explanation: Be brings 2 valence electrons and each H brings 1. They fill the two lowest orbitals, 2σ_g and 1σ_u, which are both bonding; the nonbonding 1π_u and the antibonding orbitals stay empty.

prompt: BeH2's four valence electrons fill two bonding orbitals, (2σ_g)^2(1σ_u)^2, with none in antibonding orbitals. Using bond order = (n_b − n_a)/2, what is the bond order of BeH2?
explanation: n_b = 4 and n_a = 0, so the bond order is (4 − 0)/2 = 2, as the section states: the equivalent of one bond for each Be–H link.

prompt: What does a Walsh diagram plot?

choices.text: Orbital energies against a geometry change
Photoelectron counts against kinetic energy
choices.why: That is a photoelectron spectrum (Section 10.4). A Walsh diagram plots orbital energies as a geometry coordinate, such as the bond angle, changes.

choices.text: Total energy of a molecule against temperature
choices.why: Temperature doesn't appear. A Walsh diagram follows each orbital's energy as the molecule's geometry is distorted.

choices.text: Bond order against the number of electrons
choices.why: Bond order is not plotted. A Walsh diagram plots orbital energies against a geometry coordinate, like the bond angle.

explanation: A Walsh (angular correlation) diagram plots calculated orbital energies against a distortion coordinate, such as the bond angle of an AH_2 molecule from 90° to 180°. Following the occupied orbitals shows which geometry is most stable.

prompt: According to Walsh's rule, what decides the shape a molecule adopts?

choices.text: The shape that best stabilizes its HOMO
The shape that best stabilizes its LUMO
choices.why: The LUMO is empty, so lowering it doesn't lower the molecule's energy. Walsh's rule looks at the HOMO, the highest occupied orbital.

choices.text: The shape that keeps electron pairs farthest apart
choices.why: That is the VSEPR idea. Walsh's rule is an orbital argument: the molecule takes the structure that gives its HOMO the most stability.

choices.text: The shape that leaves the most unpaired electrons
choices.why: Unpaired electrons don't decide shape in this rule. The molecule takes whatever structure best stabilizes its HOMO.

explanation: Walsh's rule says a molecule adopts the structure that provides the most stability for its highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO). The Walsh diagram shows how that orbital's energy changes with shape.

prompt: Under Walsh's rule, what decides the preferred geometry if a structural change does not affect the HOMO?

choices.text: The closest occupied orbital below the HOMO
The LUMO, the lowest empty orbital
choices.why: Empty orbitals hold no electrons, so they don't set the energy. The rule falls back on the closest occupied orbital.

choices.text: The lowest occupied orbital of all
choices.why: The deepest orbital is not the one used. The rule turns to the occupied orbital closest to the HOMO.

choices.text: Nothing; every geometry is then equally stable
choices.why: The other occupied orbitals still change with shape. The closest occupied orbital to the HOMO then governs the preferred geometry.

explanation: If a particular structural change does not perturb the HOMO, the closest occupied molecular orbital governs the preference for one geometry over another.

prompt: Walsh diagrams explain why H2O and H2S have similar shapes. What do the two molecules share that makes this work?

choices.text: The same number of valence electrons
The same total number of electrons
choices.why: H2O has 10 electrons and H2S has 18. What matters is that both have 8 valence electrons, so they fill the same orbitals on the Walsh diagram.

choices.text: Central atoms of the same size
choices.why: S is a larger atom than O. The shared feature is the same count of valence electrons, which fill the same orbitals.

choices.text: Identical bond lengths to the hydrogens
choices.why: S–H bonds are longer than O–H bonds. The likeness comes from having the same number of valence electrons.

explanation: Molecules with identical numbers of valence electrons fill the same orbitals on a Walsh diagram, so they share the same preference for shape. H2O and H2S both have 8 valence electrons: 6 from the group-16 atom and 1 from each H.

prompt: Besides comparing related molecules, what else can Walsh diagrams account for?

choices.text: Shape changes as electron count or spin changes
Shape changes when hydrogen is swapped for deuterium
choices.why: Swapping isotopes changes nuclear mass, not the orbitals, so a Walsh diagram says nothing about it. It does follow how shape changes when electrons are added or removed or the spin state changes.

choices.text: Exact bond lengths, to a hundredth of an ångström
choices.why: Walsh diagrams are qualitative; the section says they can at best tell bent from linear. They do show how shape responds to a change in electron count or spin state.

choices.text: How fast a molecule reacts with others
choices.why: Reaction rates aren't part of a Walsh diagram. It accounts for shape changes as the number of electrons or the spin state changes.

explanation: Walsh diagrams explain why related molecules with the same number of valence electrons have similar structures, and how a molecule's geometry changes when its number of electrons or its spin state changes.

prompt: According to the section, what is the most a Walsh-diagram argument can reliably tell you about water's shape?

choices.text: Whether it is bent or linear
Its bond angle to within a degree
choices.why: The method typically predicts about 90° for water, far from the measured 104°. At best it can tell a bent molecule from a linear one.

choices.text: The length of its O–H bonds
choices.why: A Walsh diagram follows orbital energies as the angle changes; it doesn't give bond lengths. At best it tells bent from linear.

choices.text: Whether it is paramagnetic
choices.why: Magnetism depends on unpaired electrons, not on the Walsh angle argument. The method's real strength is telling bent molecules from linear ones.

explanation: A typical Walsh prediction for water's bond angle is 90°, not close to the experimental value of 104°. At best, the method differentiates between a bent and a linear molecule.

prompt: In water, oxygen's orbitals are labeled by symmetry, and the 2s orbital is a_1. Which oxygen 2p orbital also carries the a_1 label?

choices.text: 2p_z
2p_x
choices.why: 2p_x, perpendicular to the molecular plane, is labeled b_1. The 2p_z orbital, which shares the symmetry of 2s, is the other a_1.

choices.text: 2p_y
choices.why: 2p_y is labeled b_2. Besides 2s, only 2p_z carries the a_1 label.

choices.text: None; only the 2s orbital is a_1
choices.why: Two oxygen orbitals are a_1: the 2s and the 2p_z. 2p_x is b_1 and 2p_y is b_2.

explanation: The oxygen orbitals are labeled a_1 (2s), b_1 (2p_x), b_2 (2p_y) and a_1 (2p_z). Because 2s and 2p_z share a symmetry, they can mix, which is why water's a_1 orbitals contain both.

prompt: Which atomic orbitals mix to form water's molecular orbitals?

choices.text: Same-symmetry orbitals of similar energy
Any orbitals at all, whatever their symmetry
choices.why: Orbitals of different symmetry have zero net overlap, so they can't mix. Mixing takes place between same-symmetry orbitals of comparable energy.

choices.text: Only orbitals on the same atom
choices.why: Mixing orbitals on one atom would give hybrids. Water's molecular orbitals mix O orbitals with H combinations of the same symmetry.

choices.text: Only orbitals of very different energy
choices.why: Orbitals far apart in energy mix very little. Mixing needs the same symmetry and comparable energies.

explanation: Mixing takes place between orbitals of the same symmetry and comparable energy. For example, oxygen's 2s and 2p_z (both a_1) mix with the in-phase H combination, which is also a_1.

prompt: Water's 1b_2 molecular orbital comes from the out-of-phase combination of the two H 1s orbitals (the hydrogen σ^* MO) mixed with which oxygen orbital?

choices.text: 2p_y
2s
choices.why: 2s has a_1 symmetry, so it can't mix with the b_2 hydrogen combination. 1b_2 comes from the O 2p_y orbital.

choices.text: 2p_x
choices.why: 2p_x is b_1 and stays nonbonding as 1b_1. The b_2 hydrogen combination mixes with 2p_y.

choices.text: 2p_z
choices.why: 2p_z is a_1 and mixes with the in-phase H combination, giving 3a_1. 1b_2 comes from 2p_y.

explanation: 1b_2 comes from mixing oxygen's 2p_y (b_2) with the out-of-phase H combination, which also has b_2 symmetry. Same-symmetry orbitals mix, and these two are the only b_2 orbitals available.

prompt: Water's 3a_1 orbital comes mainly from oxygen's 2p_z and the in-phase H combination. What does its small admixture of O 2s do?

choices.text: It weakens the bonding and raises the energy
It strengthens the bonding and lowers the energy
choices.why: That is what the small 2p_z admixture does for 2a_1. In 3a_1, the bit of 2s weakens the bonding and raises the energy.

choices.text: It turns 3a_1 into an antibonding orbital
choices.why: 3a_1 is occupied and is not antibonding; the antibonding orbitals are the empty 4a_1 and 2b_2. The small 2s admixture only weakens its bonding.

choices.text: It changes the label from a_1 to b_1
choices.why: 2s and 2p_z are both a_1, so mixing them keeps the a_1 label. The 2s admixture weakens the bonding and raises the energy.

explanation: In 3a_1 a little O 2s mixes into the O 2p_z and hydrogen combination, which weakens the bonding and raises the orbital's energy. In 2a_1 the reverse happens: a little 2p_z strengthens the bonding and lowers the energy.

prompt: What kind of orbital is water's HOMO, 1b_1?

choices.text: A nonbonding O 2p_x orbital, out of the plane
A bonding orbital spread over all three atoms
choices.why: 1b_1 has no hydrogen contribution at all. It is oxygen's 2p_x, perpendicular to the molecular plane, and is nonbonding.

choices.text: An antibonding O–H orbital
choices.why: The antibonding orbitals (4a_1 and 2b_2) are empty. The HOMO, 1b_1, is a nonbonding O 2p_x orbital.

choices.text: An in-plane lone pair made from O 2s
choices.why: 1b_1 has no 2s in it, and it isn't in the plane. It is O 2p_x, which sticks out perpendicular to the molecular plane.

explanation: 1b_1 is the nonbonding O 2p_x orbital, perpendicular to the molecular plane. It is highly localized on oxygen, much like the nonbonding orbitals of hydrogen fluoride.

prompt: The section says water's 3a_1 orbital can be thought of as a nonbonding orbital, even though it mixes O and H orbitals. Why?

choices.text: A lobe of it points away from the H atoms
It has no oxygen contribution in it at all
choices.why: 3a_1 is mostly oxygen 2p_z (0.827 in Table 10.3.1). It counts as nearly nonbonding because a large lobe points away from the H atoms.

choices.text: It is empty in the ground state
choices.why: 3a_1 is occupied; it is the next orbital below the HOMO. It counts as nearly nonbonding because it has a lobe pointing away from the hydrogens.

choices.text: It is oxygen's out-of-plane 2p_x orbital
choices.why: That is 1b_1, the HOMO. 3a_1 is built mainly from O 2p_z, with a lobe pointing away from the two H atoms.

explanation: 3a_1 lies just below the HOMO, 1b_1. It has a lobe pointing away from the two hydrogens, so its electrons do little to hold the H atoms and it can be thought of as a nonbonding orbital.

prompt: Water has 8 valence electrons (6 from O and 1 from each H), and each molecular orbital holds at most two electrons. How many of water's valence molecular orbitals are occupied in the ground state?
explanation: 8 electrons ÷ 2 per orbital = 4 filled orbitals: 2a_1, 1b_2, 3a_1 and 1b_1, giving (a_1)^2(b_2)^2(a_1)^2(b_1)^2. They are the four orbitals with negative energies in Table 10.3.1.

prompt: Suppose water were linear. Its 8 valence electrons would fill 2σ_g (2 electrons), then 1σ_u (2 electrons), then the pair of nonbonding 1π_u orbitals. How many electrons would sit in the 1π_u orbitals?
explanation: 8 − 2 − 2 = 4 electrons fill the two 1π_u orbitals, 2 in each. They would be nonbonding lone-pair electrons in oxygen's 2p_x and 2p_y.

prompt: In Table 10.3.1, which water molecular orbital has a nonzero coefficient for only one atomic orbital?

choices.why: 2a_1 mixes O 2s (0.884), O 2p_z (−0.143) and both H 1s (0.315). Only 1b_1 is a single atomic orbital, O 2p_x, with coefficient −1.000.
3a_1 mixes O 2s, O 2p_z and both H 1s orbitals. 1b_1 is the one made of O 2p_x alone.
1b_2 mixes O 2p_y with both H 1s orbitals. 1b_1, with only p_x(O) = −1.000, is the single-orbital MO.

explanation: The 1b_1 row has −1.000 under p_x(O) and zeros everywhere else, so it is purely oxygen's 2p_x: the nonbonding, out-of-plane lone pair.

prompt: In Table 10.3.1, every b orbital (1b_1, 1b_2 and 2b_2) has a coefficient of zero for s(O). Why?

choices.text: O 2s is a_1, so it can't mix into b orbitals
O 2s is too low in energy to mix with anything
choices.why: O 2s does mix strongly; it is the main part of 2a_1 (0.884). It is missing from the b orbitals only because its symmetry is a_1.

choices.text: The b orbitals are all antibonding
choices.why: 1b_2 is bonding and 1b_1 nonbonding; only 2b_2 is antibonding. The zeros come from symmetry: O 2s is a_1.

choices.text: The b orbitals are all empty
choices.why: 1b_1 and 1b_2 are occupied; only 2b_2 is empty. The zeros come from symmetry, since O 2s is a_1.

explanation: Only orbitals of the same symmetry mix. Oxygen's 2s is a_1, so it appears in the a_1 orbitals (2a_1, 3a_1 and 4a_1) and has a zero coefficient in every b orbital.

prompt: Table 10.3.1 gives water's HOMO (1b_1) an energy of −12.191 and its LUMO (4a_1) an energy of 5.440, in the same units. What is the HOMO–LUMO gap, in those units?
explanation: Gap = E(LUMO) − E(HOMO) = 5.440 − (−12.191) = 17.631. The HOMO is the highest of the four occupied (negative-energy) orbitals, and the LUMO is the lower of the two empty ones.
